label: token right after an early j (step 1 or 2)
explanation: Fires only in the original phase, at step 1 or 2, when the previous input was j (orig(0) or orig(1) == j). It fires every time this holds (precision 1.0) and the condition covers 99% of activation mass. Magnitude is about 0.58 of max at step 1 (j first) and about 0.63-1.0 at step 2, peaking at max for the prefix g j. Does not depend on the current token. Never fires at step 0, at step 3 or later, on the delimiter, or in the copy phase, and does not fire for a j later in the sequence. Missed activations are tiny (<0.1 of max) and occur at step 2 after other prefixes, mostly ones starting with g.

issues: The factual claims hold up. The phase breakdown shows zero activations in the delimiter and copy phases and at t=0. There are only 2 activations at t=3 (out of 500k steps) and none later. On the test split, precision is 1.0 and mass recall is 0.991.
The two halves of the predicate split as described. (t==1)&(orig(0)==j) has precision 1.0 and mass 0.437. (t==2)&(orig(1)==j) has precision 1.0 and mass 0.554.

The misses (2849 test steps, 0.9% of mass) are all at step 2 and tiny (0.01-0.13 of max), often after prefixes starting with g. This is not a usable class: (t==2)&(orig(0)==g)&(orig(1)!=j) has precision 0.13 and covers only 0.86% of mass. That makes it low-magnitude leakage, not a missed concept.

Minor nuance: 'does not depend on the current token' is slightly overstated for magnitude. All top-activating examples are 'g j [d:1.00]', and step-2 examples with current token d run higher (0.63-0.70) than ones with other tokens (about 0.58-0.59). Whether the feature fires does not depend on the current token, but the current token d appears to raise its magnitude.
